summary_en: How do people perceive their own position in the income distribution, and how does that perception relate to actual inequality? Cervone, Gáspár and co-authors propose a 'twofold-subjective' Gini coefficient that combines respondents' perceived ladder-position with their guesses about the distribution shape. Using survey data from many countries they show this twofold measure tracks objective inequality more closely than earlier single-question subjective Ginis, and uncovers systematic differences in how rich and poor respondents misperceive the distribution.
data_used: International survey data on respondents' perceived income position (ladder-rung self-placement) and beliefs about the shape of the income distribution; comparison with WIID / SWIID / OECD measures of objective Gini coefficients across countries.
policy_relevance: Useful methodological input for Hungarian inequality-perception surveys (KSH attitudes module, ESS Hungary) and for any government communication on inequality / redistribution policy: subjective inequality measures matter for political support of tax-and-transfer reforms, and the paper provides a sharper tool for measuring them. Particularly relevant for the design of Hungarian KSH survey modules on perceived welfare position.
title: A Twofold-Subjective Measure of Income Inequality
